outcomes.original: Filing step: Secure a Type 47 license in escrow: identify an existing Type 47 license available for premises-to-premises transfer, negotiate purchase (expect $100k–$450k in San Francisco), and open escrow with an ABC-licensed broker. What to say: The Type 47 license is a quota license that cannot be newly issued in San Francisco; you must purchase an existing one. Engage a license broker immediately, before filing anything with the city. Make the lease and the CUA application contingent on ABC approving the transfer. The broker will prepare the ABC-257 (Application for Transfer of License) and coordinate with the seller. Budget 4–8 months for the full transfer process after ABC approval.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Register the business with the San Francisco Treasurer & Tax Collector to obtain a Business Account Number (BAN) and business registration certificate. What to say: Every other city department requires the BAN before accepting an application. Register online at sftreasurer.org within 30 days of starting business; fee is tiered by gross receipts ($55–$700 plus $4 state fee). Print the certificate; Planning, ABC, and DPH will ask for it. If the public-facing name differs from the legal entity name, file a Fictitious Business Name statement with the County Clerk and publish it.

outcomes.original: Filing step: File the Conditional Use Authorization application with San Francisco Planning, requesting authorization under § 780.3(c)(2)(A) for a restaurant serving full liquor (Type 47) as a bona fide eating place. What to say: Prepare the CUA application with site photos, floor plan showing dining area and kitchen, menu, and a narrative explaining that the space has operated as a restaurant since at least 1986, currently holds Type 41, and will maintain at least 51% of gross receipts from food. Attach the ABC escrow agreement and the prior CUA approvals (1986.553C, 1998.409C, 2010.0514C) to show the site's history. Commit to providing gross-receipts records to Planning on request. Address the undue-concentration issue by showing the bona fide eating place operation serves neighborhood convenience. The CUA fee in 2022 was approximately $2,747 for no-construction cases, CPI-adjusted annually; confirm the current fee with Planning. Budget 4–10 months to hearing and decision.
outcomes.note: The cited records are agency referrals at different addresses (431 and 362 Columbus Ave); none supports the filing requirements, fees, timeline, or historical facts about 414 Columbus Ave.

outcomes.original: Filing step: After the Planning Commission approves the CUA and it becomes final (30 days after the decision if no appeal), submit the ABC Type 47 transfer application (ABC-257) with the signed CUA motion as the zoning clearance. What to say: ABC requires a local agency clearance before issuing the license; the approved CUA motion satisfies that requirement. Submit the ABC-257 with the seller's information, the signed lease, the seller's permit, the CUA motion, proof of workers' compensation insurance, and the transfer fee. ABC will send the application to SFPD and Planning for referral review, post public notice at the premises for 30 days, and investigate. If the census tract is over-concentrated, ABC may require a Public Convenience or Necessity finding from the city; coordinate with the district supervisor's office if ABC requests it. Budget 3–8 months for ABC to issue the license after the application is deemed complete.
outcomes.supported_text: Budget 3–8 months for ABC to issue the license after the application is deemed complete.

outcomes.original: Filing step: File for the Health Permit to Operate with SF Department of Public Health, submitting the BAN, Location ID (LIN), menu, and proof of a certified food safety manager on staff. What to say: Apply online at least one month before opening. The $470 application fee includes the initial inspection; the annual license fee for restaurants is $0 for 2026–28 under the current fee schedule. DPH will refer the application to Planning for zoning confirmation. Schedule the pre-opening inspection when the space is 100% ready: equipment installed, finishes complete, hot water working, hand sinks in place. Failed inspections push opening by 2–3 weeks, so walk the DPH checklist in advance. If the space or equipment has changed since the last operator, you may need a plan check; confirm with DPH whether the existing approved plans cover your operation.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Obtain RBS (Responsible Beverage Service) certification for every alcohol server and manager, and food handler cards for all food employees, before opening. What to say: California requires RBS certification within 60 days of hire for anyone serving alcohol (register at ABC's RBS Portal, $3, complete an approved course for about $10–$25, pass the exam). Food handler cards are required within 30 days of hire (online ANSI-accredited course, $7–$15, valid 3 years). At least one employee must hold a Certified Food Protection Manager certificate (ServSafe or equivalent, $100–$250, valid 5 years); DPH asks for it at the pre-opening inspection. Keep the certification list on site for ABC and DPH inspections.

outcomes.original: Estimated time: 120 to 300 days. Estimated government cost: $3,200 to $453,000. Notes: This range is the time and government cost to obtain the Conditional Use Authorization, the ABC Type 47 transfer, and the Health Permit to Operate, when they are granted. The CUA typically takes 120–300 days from filing to final (including pre-application, hearing scheduling, the 30-day appeal period, and any continuances); the ABC Type 47 transfer adds 90–240 days after the CUA is final, depending on escrow, public notice, referral review, and whether a Public Convenience or Necessity finding is required for the over-concentrated census tract; and the health permit takes 14–45 days after application when the space is inspection-ready. Government costs include the CUA filing fee (approximately $2,750–$3,150 in 2022, CPI-adjusted annually), the ABC Type 47 transfer application fee ($17,000 baseline, but the license itself costs $100,000–$450,000 to purchase on the open market in San Francisco, which is not a government fee but is the dominant cost), and the DPH permit-to-operate application ($470). These figures exclude the building permit (no construction stated), sign permit, business registration ($55–$700), seller's permit and EIN (free), RBS and food safety certifications ($110–$295 per person), and workers' compensation insurance premiums. The total calendar time from starting the CUA application to pouring the first legal drink under the Type 47 license is realistically 10–20 months. The day range is for approvals; a denial or withdrawal takes less time but has no predictable range because the records do not show when denied or withdrawn cases stop.
